Article Title: A former St. Louis department-store warehouse is slated to become a 525,000-square-foot data centre as part of a $3.1 billion district; residents are fighting the 120-megawatt project in court
Article Text:
The future vision

A resisting community

A strong developer

Halting data centre development

A larger fight

In the never-ending race to keep US at the centre of all global development, a fight has ensued between citizens and developers. While previously one could spot a cafe or grocery store at short intervals in America, it has now been replaced with a data centre at every turn. While some have willingly sold their land for the development of these hubs, others have been forced to do so by the townships. All of this, because the deemed "futuristic" data centres are necessary to support the massive computing power required by AI and fulfil the dreams of the world's rich.One such city whose landscape is currently changing day by day is America's brewing capital, St. Louis. The city is seeking to reinvent itself as a tech hub by planning a sprawling new technology park anchored by a giant data centre, a project that is already facing public backlash and legal battles, according to Realtor.com.A city of roughly 280,000 people, St. Louis already hosts more than a dozen operational data centres, with three more currently under construction in the area and up to 10 more in various stages of planning. Among the most controversial of these is the 120-megawatt, 525,000-square-foot hyperscale facility slated for Midtown St. Louis. The chosen site previously housed a Macy's and Famous Barr warehouse adjacent to the historic Armory building.The data centre, co-developed by TeraWatt Infrastructure—a San Francisco–based company that specialises in commercial electric vehicle-charging networks—is envisioned as the linchpin of the privately funded $3.1 billion Armory Innovation District. Located alongside Interstate Highway 64, the long-vacant Armory building, which previously housed a tennis training centre, an entertainment complex and a sports venue, is poised to be converted into 214,500 square feet of high-tech office and creative space.According to developer statements, the district project will create more than 1,000 temporary union construction jobs and 200 permanent on-site positions. Prohibited from seeking tax abatements, the centre is projected to generate $432 million in tax revenue over its first decade, with nearly half of the amount going to St. Louis public schools.If development proceeds on schedule, construction will get underway in August 2027 and conclude by late 2029. Supporters of the project say it will give the local economy a shot in the arm. "Data centres allow communities to repopulate the middle class," Ron Kitchens, CEO of Greater St. Louis, the metro's leading economic development organisation championing the Armory project and other local data centres, told Realtor.com. According to Kitchens, data centres like the TeraWatt development are a boon to the local housing market because they create well-paying jobs for local residents without consuming land that could have been used for residential construction. "We have housing demand coming on because we have electricians making $80,000," argued Kitchens. "Families that could not talk about homeownership now have access to it."The Armory Innovation District and the adjacent data centre have secured key municipal approvals, including a conditional use permit and a community benefits agreement. Under that agreement, developers are required to contribute $15.75 million toward infrastructure, digital access, job retraining for workers affected by artificial intelligence, and environmental justice activities.However, opposition over bringing a data centre to Midtown St. Louis has led to legal action on both sides. In August, opponent groups filed a lawsuit challenging the project's use permit, claiming that the decision to grant it was made "contrary to law.""These hyperscale data centres are not welcome in St. Louis, and the residents are going to continue to fight tooth and nail at every chance we get to stop them," plaintiff Kerry McCullen told St. Louis Public Radio at the time.Fellow plaintiff Daniel Pate claimed that potential negative health and environmental risks related to data centres were not thoroughly studied and taken into account before the project was green-lit by the city. "The city is bending and twisting themselves into pretzels to try to get this thing through," Pate said.In retaliation, just weeks later, TeraWatt, the company behind the Midtown data centre, filed its own lawsuit against the city of St. Louis, reported St. Louis Public Radio. In the complaint, TeraWatt partner David Lambiaso alleged that two conditions the Board of Adjustment imposed as prerequisites for the construction are illegal and exceed "the scope of authority" of the board.According to the lawsuit, forcing the data centre to use 2.4 MWs of renewable energy would be "practically impossible" on the 11-acre site. Lambiaso also took issue with a provision requiring the city’s Board of Aldermen to approve the community benefits agreement.In response to local protests and months of heated debates, St. Louis in September enacted a set of rules restricting future data centre construction and operation within city limits, reported the station KSDK. Signed into law by Mayor Cara Spencer, the legislation establishes buffer zones between data centres and sensitive areas like residential neighbourhoods and schools, imposes caps on noise levels, and requires facilities to transition to renewable energy over time. Alderwoman Anne Schweitzer, who co-sponsored the bill touted by Spencer as "nation-leading," acknowledged that while the rules provide important safeguards, they fall short of addressing every concern."It doesn't stop data centres from being allowed in the city of St. Louis," Schweitzer said. "It doesn't prevent every single harm that could be caused. It doesn't protect ratepayers from the increases in their utility bills that we should expect."While Kitchens acknowledged that people's anxiety about the impact of AI on their employment is not unfounded, he believes the technology will create new opportunities that never existed before. Consequently, stalling local development is a losing strategy."Should there be regulation of AI? Probably, but not building a data centre in Missouri and building in Taipei or Chile doesn’t stop AI. It just stops prosperity," he argues. "We’re going to lose twice."The backlash against data centres is not limited to St. Louis. The rapid expansion of infrastructure necessary to support AI buildout has been a highly controversial and opposed topic in the United States for the past few years. Surging electricity rates, grid strain, high water consumption for cooling systems, noise pollution near residential areas, along with the broader suspicion of AI, have united people. In May, Gallup’s first poll on data centre construction found 71% of Americans oppose AI data centres in their local area.The technology remains unregulated at the federal level, despite recent high-profile appeals for guardrails and safety controls from industry leaders, including Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman.
Article Summary: America's brewing capital, St. Louis, is seeking to reinvent itself as a tech hub. The city is planning a sprawling new technology park anchored by a giant data centre. The project is already facing public backlash and legal battles. Supporters of the project say it will give the local economy a shot in the arm.

Article Title: In 1940, a Jewish family's Kandinsky painting was sold under Nazi occupation; 83 years later, their heirs recovered it, and it has now fetched £31.56 million at a London auction after decades of dispu
Article Text:
Kandinsky painting sold under Nazi occupation returns to heirs, fetches £31.56m at London auction (Image Credit: Instagram/ @ art__window)

A painting caught in the turmoil of the Second World War

From private ownership to a German museum

Restitution after 83 years

A record result at Christie's London auction

A painting by Russian artist Wassily Kandinsky, sold under disputed circumstances during Nazi occupation in 1940, has fetched £31.56 million at a London auction, bringing renewed attention to one family's decades-long struggle to recover its artwork. The painting, Das bunte Leben (The Colorful Life), was returned to the heirs of its original Jewish owners in 2023, 83 years after the wartime sale. According to auction house Christie's, the 1907 masterpiece became the highest-value lot of its London evening sale on October 14, 2026, following nearly six minutes of competitive bidding.Das bunte Leben was acquired in November 1927 by Hedwig and Emanuel Albert Lewenstein, a Jewish couple who lived in Amsterdam and collected art. The painting was subsequently loaned to the city's Stedelijk Museum in 1933, where it remained on public display. The couple died before the Second World War, leaving their art collection to their two children. Both children left Europe before or during the early stages of the conflict as Nazi Germany's persecution of Jewish people intensified.On October 9, 1940, the Kandinsky painting was sold at an auction in Amsterdam.The sale took place less than five months after German forces occupied the Netherlands. Questions surrounding the circumstances of the transaction later became central to the family's efforts to reclaim the artwork. According to The Times of Israel, the painting was purchased by Salomon Slijper, a Dutch Jewish businessman who survived the war in hiding. The circumstances of the sale remained disputed for decades. Bayerische Landesbank argued that Irma Lewenstein Klein had initiated the auction in connection with a divorce dispute, but the German Advisory Commission found insufficient evidence to establish that she had voluntarily submitted the painting for sale.The painting changed hands again in 1972, following Slijper's death. His widow, Johanna, sold it to Bayerische Landesbank, the state bank of Bavaria, for 900,000 Dutch guilders. The bank subsequently lent the artwork to the Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus and Kunstbau museum in Munich, Germany. It remained associated with the institution for approximately five decades, while the Lewenstein family continued to pursue its claim to the painting.In 2017, the family's heirs filed a lawsuit seeking its return. Their claim formed part of the broader effort to recover artworks lost through Nazi persecution, forced sales and other transactions during the Holocaust. Such cases can be difficult to resolve because they involve records of historical ownership, the circumstances in which an artwork changed hands and the legal status of subsequent purchases. In this case, the question was whether the 1940 sale could be considered legitimate given the persecution of Jewish people under Nazi occupation.A significant development came in May 2023, when an independent German commission concluded that Das bunte Leben had been lost as a result of the persecution of Jews under German occupation. It recommended that the painting be returned to the Lewenstein heirs. Bayerische Landesbank implemented the recommendation in June 2023, restoring the artwork to the family after decades of uncertainty. The restitution allowed the heirs to regain control of the painting and eventually offer it for sale.The case also illustrates the continuing importance of restitution processes in addressing the legacy of Nazi-looted art. Although the return of an artwork cannot reverse the circumstances in which it was lost, it can acknowledge the injustice suffered by its original owners and their descendants.The painting's return to the market culminated in its sale at Christie's London auction on October 14, 2026. It achieved £31,560,000, equivalent to approximately $42 million, after almost six minutes of bidding. Christie's reported that the work exceeded its pre-sale estimate of £18 million to £25 million, making it the leading lot of the evening's 20th/21st Century London Evening Sale. The auction house described the painting as an important early work in Kandinsky's artistic development.Painted in 1907, Das bunte Leben depicts a colourful, panoramic scene featuring figures gathered in a landscape, with a walled town crowning a hill in the distance. Its vivid palette and narrative imagery reflect an earlier phase of Kandinsky's career, before his move towards greater abstraction. The sale took place as part of a wider evening of auctions that generated approximately £218.6 million across Christie's combined London sales. According to the auction house, the Kandinsky painting was the highest-value lot of the evening. The identity of the buyer was not disclosed. Beyond its financial value, the painting's journey from a disputed wartime sale to restitution and a multimillion-pound auction underscores how the history of an artwork can remain inseparable from the lives of the people who once owned it.
Article Summary: Das bunte Leben (The Colorful Life) was sold at an auction in Amsterdam in 1940. It was purchased by Salomon Slijper, a Dutch Jewish businessman who survived the war in hiding. The circumstances of the sale remained disputed for decades. In 2023, an independent German commission concluded the painting had been lost as a result of the persecution of Jews under German occupation. It recommended that the painting be returned to the Lewenstein heirs.

Article Title: At 14, Oregon teenager Elijah Buckwald climbed onto an overturned pickup to help free an elderly couple trapped inside; two years later, at 16, he received Scouting America’s Honor Medal for lifesavin
Article Text:
At 16, Elijah Buckwald received Scouting America’s Honor Medal for lifesaving heroism after helping rescue an elderly couple.

A crash on Santiam Pass

Recognition for a lifesaving act

When training meets instinct

Some moments leave little time for hesitation. For Elijah Buckwald, a routine drive through Oregon’s Santiam Pass became one of those moments when, at just 14, he found himself standing on an overturned pickup truck, helping strangers trapped inside after a serious crash. Two years later, that instinct to step forward has earned the Redmond teenager national recognition, states an online report by KTVZ21 News.According to the report, in August 2024, Buckwald was travelling with his grandparents near the summit of Santiam Pass when they encountered an overturned pickup truck and camper trailer blocking the highway. Inside the wreckage was an elderly couple who needed help.With emergency responders yet to arrive, Buckwald got out to assess the situation. He climbed onto the overturned pickup, reached the passenger side and opened the door. He then held it in place while other adults worked to get the couple safely out of the vehicle.The quick response helped create an opening for the trapped occupants to be brought to safety. Despite the severity of the crash, neither person was injured.For Buckwald, who was only 14 at the time, the situation called for action rather than waiting for someone else to take charge, adds the online report.Now 16 and a member of Scout Troop 25, Buckwald has been recognised with Scouting America’s prestigious Honor Medal, a national award presented to Scouts and adult leaders for acts of heroism and lifesaving service, also adds the report.The honour places his actions on Santiam Pass among the organisation’s recognised examples of courage and preparedness. It also highlights how skills developed through Scouting can become valuable in unexpected, real-world emergencies.Buckwald’s actions were carried out before professional first responders reached the scene, making his willingness to help particularly significant, informs the report too.The incident has also become a point of pride for Buckwald’s troop, where preparedness and service are central parts of the Scouting experience. His actions demonstrated how training can translate into calm decision-making when circumstances suddenly become dangerous.What began as an ordinary journey with his grandparents ultimately became a defining moment for the teenager. At an age when most people might have stood back and waited for help, Buckwald moved towards the overturned vehicle and helped make a dangerous situation safer.His recognition two years later serves as a reminder that heroism does not always arrive with dramatic gestures.Images Courtesy: Facebook and KTVZ21 News
Article Summary: Elijah Buckwald, then 14, helped rescue an elderly couple trapped in an overturned pickup truck on Oregon's Santiam Pass. At 16, he received Scouting America’s Honor Medal for lifesaving heroism. The award is presented to Scouts and adult leaders for acts of heroism and lifesaving service.

Article Title: NBA coach Tyronn Lue turns a former segregated school in his hometown into a community centre as part of his $10 million commitment
Article Text:
PC: NBA

How Garfield School went from a segregated school to a community hub

Tyronn Lue's $10 million commitment to the community

Kim and Olivia Lue Garfield Legacy Center honours family history

Tyronn Lue’s C2C initiative looks beyond Garfield School’s dedication

In Mexico, Missouri, a former school building has taken on a new role after years away from its original purpose. Garfield School, once established to educate Black children during segregation, is now the headquarters of a community initiative founded by Los Angeles Clippers head coach Tyronn Lue. The project brings the historic property back into community use, with education and youth support among its priorities. According to PRNewswire, in July 2025, the building was formally dedicated under a new name honouring Lue's mother and grandmother. The change forms part of a wider $10 million commitment to the town, where Lue grew up and where the school remains part of the area's history.Garfield School was established during the era of racial segregation in the United States, when Black pupils were educated in separate facilities. Its place in Mexico's history extended beyond the classroom, with generations of local families connected to the institution.The school eventually closed and the property was later used by a credit union. Its educational role had ended, leaving a building whose original purpose was tied to a different period in the town's past. Lue's decision to acquire the property created an opportunity to return it to community use, this time through programmes intended to support young people and connect residents with local resources.For Lue, the building also carried a personal connection. He grew up in Mexico, Missouri, and has spoken about the influence of the wider community on his upbringing. The school had been important to local residents, and its closure had been a source of disappointment for people who remembered its earlier role.Reportedly, the former school is now the base for Commitment to Community (C2C), a $10 million initiative established by Lue. The project is intended to support the Mexico area through educational opportunities, youth programming and partnerships with organisations working in the community.The initiative is being developed in collaboration with the Tyronn Lue Fund and Partners for Rural Impact, a national non-profit organisation focused on expanding educational opportunities in rural communities. The partnership brings together Lue's investment in his hometown and an organisation with experience in supporting young people and families.The school is one part of the broader effort. Buildings next to the property, which had also been acquired from a local credit union, are expected to be adapted for youth activities, resource centres and other community services. These spaces are intended to complement the work based at the former school, giving the initiative room to expand its activities.At a dedication ceremony held in early July 2025, Lue announced that the building would be known as the Kim and Olivia Lue Garfield Legacy Center. The name recognises his mother and grandmother, as well as their connection to Garfield School.The event brought together community members, local leaders and former students. A ribbon-cutting ceremony marked the change, while a community legacy walk and tours of nearby buildings gave attendees an opportunity to see the developing project.The renaming places Lue's family history alongside the school's longer history in Mexico. Rather than being used solely as a headquarters for a charitable initiative, the property is intended to remain connected to the people it serves, with educational programming and local partnerships at the centre of its new role.The July dedication marked an early milestone for C2C, rather than the completion of its work. Plans for the surrounding properties include dedicated areas for youth programmes and community services, while partnerships are expected to help deliver educational opportunities for local families.The initiative also has a fundraising component beyond Missouri. Lue planned to bring attention to the project at the second annual C2C fundraising event for October 19, 2025, at the Intuit Dome in California, the home arena of the Los Angeles Clippers. The event was intended to help support the initiative's wider work.The transformation of Garfield School links the project's future plans with a building that already holds a place in local history. Established to serve Black students during segregation, later used by a credit union and now serving as the home of C2C, the property has passed through several distinct phases. Its latest role centres on education, youth support and community resources in the town where Lue was raised.
Article Summary: Garfield School was established during the era of racial segregation in the U.S. It was later used by a credit union, leaving a building whose original purpose was tied to a different period in the town's past. In July 2025, the building was formally dedicated under a new name honouring Lue's mother and grandmother. The former school is now the base for Commitment to Community (C2C), a $10 million initiative established by Lue.

Article Title: Radio tags reveal how giant green anacondas hide underwater in the Amazon; researchers spotted them at just 17.7% of tracked locations
Article Text:
Representative Image of a green anaconda concealed among dense vegetation and riverbanks in the western Amazon rainforest (AI-generated image)

How researchers tracked four green anacondas in Peru

Where green anacondas bask and hide

Why hidden snakes complicate population surveys

In the western Amazon , finding a green anaconda can depend on more than knowing which river it inhabits. Dense vegetation, submerged debris and concealed riverbanks can make the giant reptile difficult to observe, even when researchers are tracking its movements. A study published in the Journal of Natural History in 2025 has documented how the giant reptiles use waterways and surrounding vegetation in the western Amazon. In Habitat use of cryptic Green Anaconda (Eunectes murinus) in the western Amazon , researchers compiled 180 observations involving at least 50 individual snakes in Peru’s Madre de Dios region. Four adults were fitted with very-high-frequency radio tags and tracked. At just 23 of their recorded radio locations, or 17.7%, were the snakes visible without disturbance. The findings show why the animals’ tendency to remain concealed, emerging into view mainly to bask, matters when researchers attempt to locate them and estimate their populations.The research brought together habitat records from several collaborating projects in the Madre de Dios region of southeastern Peru. The observations came mainly from three methods: opportunistic encounters, intensive surveys and radio telemetry.The study’s results and supplementary records also include a small number of observations from general fauna surveys. The researchers recorded 180 observations involving at least 50 individual E. murinus, with telemetry tracking accounting for 130 records, or 72.2% of the total. The fieldwork covered a variety of aquatic environments, including rivers, streams, oxbow lakes and aguajales. An aguajal is a wetland dominated by aguaje palms, known scientifically as Mauritia flexuosa. The tagged snakes were tracked along the Los Amigos, Las Piedras and Madre de Dios rivers. The wider dataset included observations from additional river systems and wetland habitats across the region.Radio telemetry allowed researchers to locate tagged snakes even when vegetation, submerged logs or riverbanks obscured them from view. Capturing the larger snakes required substantial personnel and experience. The researchers described using a team of at least four people when handling particularly large individuals. Capture attempts depended on whether suitable personnel were available and whether the circumstances allowed the animal to be handled safely. The four tagged animals were adults. Their tracking records provided detailed information about where the snakes rested, basked and remained concealed across different habitats. However, the 180 observations were not all tracking records, and the results should be understood as a combination of telemetry data and other field observations.The study found that green anacondas in the western Amazon were typically exposed when basking, while remaining partly or entirely concealed at most other tracked locations. Their hiding places included fallen logs, accumulated leaf litter and other detritus, submerged vegetation, fallen palm trunks and undercut riverbanks. On one occasion, a tracked snake was found inside a burrow of unknown origin. Basking sites varied by habitat. Along rivers, log jams appeared to be the preferred places for basking. In aguajales and oxbow lakes, the snakes used well-vegetated embankments and fixed or floating mats of vegetation. The researchers also found that the animals rarely occupied streams, although they sometimes used connecting waterways and seasonally flooded areas.Individual tracking records illustrate how much these habitats can vary. One female weighed 100 kg and had a snout-to-vent length of 486 cm, with a further 77 cm measured along her tail. Her records placed her most often in closed-canopy aguajal habitat, while the remaining observations were from grass mats in open water. These records show that the tracked snake used more than one type of aquatic environment. A tracked male was also found in temporarily flooded forest, where he was nearly invisible in shallow pools beneath dense vegetation. In one observation, he was concealed beneath leaf litter and shallow water, with only his nostrils exposed. Such records help explain why a snake’s location may be known through telemetry even when a researcher cannot readily see the animal.The findings also fit with earlier research on anacondas and mineral licks. A separate 2024 study, Does the Southern Green Anaconda, Eunectes murinus, seek areas of high prey concentration in southeastern Peru? , described predation at mineral licks and associations between known mineral-lick locations and three radio-tagged snakes. Its authors suggested that anacondas may target such sites because prey can congregate there. This is related evidence about hunting behaviour, rather than a result that should be attributed solely to the 2025 habitat study.The most important implication is for wildlife surveys. If researchers count only the snakes they can see from riverbanks or boats, they may miss animals concealed beneath vegetation, submerged debris or riverbanks. The finding that tagged snakes were visible without disturbance at only 17.7% of their radio locations shows how rarely these four adults were observed in the open at their recorded positions. The authors identify basking behaviour as an important factor when evaluating population densities from survey detections. They report that, in most of the habitats surveyed, anacondas were easily detected and best positioned for safe capture when basking. The study nevertheless has limits. Only four adult snakes were radio-tagged, and the work focused on one region of Peru. The results cannot establish that all green anacondas, including juveniles and animals in other parts of South America, use habitats in precisely the same way.Taxonomy is another consideration. A 2024 genetic study, Disentangling the Anacondas: Revealing a New Green Species and Rethinking Yellows , proposed recognising the northern green anaconda as Eunectes akayima, distinct from the southern green anaconda, Eunectes murinus. The 2025 study concerns E. murinus in Peru and should not automatically be taken as describing the behaviour of both proposed species. The central finding is straightforward: green anacondas can occupy waterways and wetlands while remaining difficult to detect, even when researchers know their locations. By combining radio tracking with other field observations, the study provides a clearer account of how these giant snakes use their habitats and why finding them in the wild remains a challenge.
Article Summary: Researchers compiled 180 observations involving at least 50 individual snakes in Peru’s Madre de Dios region. Four adults were fitted with very-high-frequency radio tags and tracked. At just 23 of their recorded radio locations, or 17.7%, were the snakes visible without disturbance.

Article Title: In 1975, Kodak began operating a uranium-based research device beneath its Rochester laboratory; 31 years later it shut down, and a new account explains why it was never a self-sustaining nuclear reac
Article Text:
Kodak's equipment contained about 3.5 pounds of highly enriched uranium (Representational AP photo)

Why did Kodak need nuclear equipment?

Why was Kodak's machine different from a nuclear reactor?

How did the public find out about the device?

For most people, Kodak is a name associated with cameras and photographic film. But for 31 years, the American company had something far less familiar inside its research facility in Rochester, New York: a nuclear device containing highly enriched uranium.The machine began operating in 1975 and remained in use until 2006. Its existence attracted widespread attention only in 2012, years after it had shut down. Now, a report by Popular Mechanics, published on Wednesday, has revisited the unusual facility and explained why the equipment, despite using uranium, was not a self-sustaining nuclear reactor.The machine was about the size of a refrigerator and was kept in a secure underground laboratory. According to the report, it was not being used to produce electricity or develop nuclear weapons. Kodak's scientists, however, used it to examine materials, identify unwanted substances in chemicals, and look inside objects without damaging them.The equipment was known as a californium neutron flux multiplier, or CFX, whose purpose was to produce a supply of neutrons, tiny particles found inside atoms, which scientists could use to study different materials.What later drew attention was the uranium inside the machine. Highly enriched uranium can also be used in nuclear weapons, raising questions about why a photography company had access to it. However, the device had operated under government supervision, and its existence had been mentioned in scientific papers even though Kodak had not widely publicised it.Kodak's work involved more than making cameras and selling photographic film. The company also carried out research into the materials and chemicals used in its products. Scientists needed to check what those materials contained and whether unwanted substances were present.The nuclear device helped them do this in two ways. The first was a process called neutron activation analysis. Scientists directed neutrons at a sample, causing some of its atoms to release signals in the form of gamma rays. By measuring those signals, researchers could identify the elements present in the material. This allowed them to detect impurities.The second method, neutron radiography, helped scientists examine the inside of an object without cutting it open.This makes neutron imaging useful for examining certain lighter materials, including water and photographic film, that may not show up clearly in ordinary X-ray images.The machine used two radioactive materials to produce the neutrons needed for its experiments. One was californium-252, a substance that naturally releases neutrons. The device contained only about 3.1 milligrams of it. These neutrons then travelled through 52 plates containing highly enriched uranium.When neutrons struck some of the uranium atoms, the atoms split and released more neutrons. This process is called nuclear fission.The arrangement allowed Kodak to produce a much larger supply of neutrons than californium alone could provide. According to the report, the number could increase by as much as 30 times.But the machine could not keep this process going by itself. It depended on californium to supply the neutrons needed to start and maintain the reactions, or the reaction would gradually stop.Kodak operated the machine for more than three decades. During that period, its californium source was replaced approximately every seven years so the equipment could continue functioning.The device was housed behind thick protective walls and operated under government-approved security arrangements. Although it was used for research, the company did not widely publicise its presence.The story reached a much larger audience in 2012, when information about the facility appeared in local news reports.According to an Associated Press report published in May 2012, Kodak's equipment contained about 3.5 pounds of highly enriched uranium. The report also confirmed that the machine had been used for examining materials and producing images.By then, however, the device was no longer operating. Kodak had stopped using it in 2006, and the uranium was removed in 2007 during the dismantling process. The material was transferred to a federal facility under strict security arrangements.The former laboratory was later declared safe, although small amounts of radioactive isotopes had been activated in the concrete surrounding the equipment. The building has since been sold by Kodak.
Article Summary: Kodak's equipment contained about 3.5 pounds of highly enriched uranium. It was not being used to produce electricity or develop nuclear weapons. Scientists used it to examine materials, identify unwanted substances in chemicals, and look inside objects without damaging them. The machine began operating in 1975 and remained in use until 2006.

Article Title: Explosion, fuel leak: Two Syrian pipelines damaged in fresh blow to war-hit energy network
Article Text:
Security forces of Syria's Interior Ministry guard the al-Omar oil field, the country's largest by area and production

Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday, with one explosion triggering a fire and another causing a fuel leak, Syrian state media reported.According to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), citing the state-owned Syrian Petroleum Company, an explosion struck the Jbessa gas pipeline in Hasakah province, while a separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.The explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze.The Syrian Petroleum Company described the incident as sabotage. Officials said alternative arrangements would maintain gas supplies to power stations during repairs, while domestic gas supplies remained unaffected.In a separate incident, a hole was discovered in the Baniyas-Homs pipeline in the Hadida area west of Homs, causing a leak of petroleum products. Emergency and technical teams were deployed to contain the leak and isolate the damaged section.Al Jazeera, citing Syrian state media, reported that the damage to the Baniyas-Homs pipeline was believed to be linked to an attempted fuel theft. The initial reports did not confirm the cause or identify those responsible.The incidents come amid a series of disruptions to Syria’s energy infrastructure. Earlier in October, an oil pipeline near Tal Hamis in Hasakah province was damaged in what the Syrian Petroleum Company described as sabotage.Syria is working to rebuild its oil and gas infrastructure after years of conflict, restoring production in northeastern oilfields and reconnecting them with processing facilities and refineries in Homs and Baniyas.In January 2026, the Syrian Petroleum Company began pumping raw gas from the Jbessa fields in Hasakah to the Furqlus gas plant in Homs countryside at around 1.2 million cubic metres per day to support electricity generation.The second damaged pipeline, connecting Baniyas on the Mediterranean coast to Homs, transports petroleum products between two important energy centres. The Baniyas refinery is undergoing an overhaul aimed at increasing its processing capacity from around 80,000 to 130,000 barrels per day.Syria has also undertaken emergency pipeline repairs and plans to expand its transportation network. A September 2026 analysis by the Baker Institute for Public Policy reported that the Syrian Petroleum Company was repairing existing infrastructure and planning a heavy-crude pipeline linking northeastern oilfields to the Baniyas refinery.
Article Summary: Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday. One explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze. A separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.

Article Title: SFJ chief Gurpatwant Singh Pannun claims FBI warned him of fresh threat ahead of Canada visit
Article Text:
FBI, Gurpatwant Singh Pannun

Article Title: Texas took their land for a highway, changed the route and left part unused; now the owners want to buy it back
Article Text:
Representative image

How Texas acquired the property

The case reached the Texas Supreme Court

What the Supreme Court ruled

What Texas law says about buying back condemned land

The Texas Supreme Court has ruled that a claim to buy back land acquired for a highway can proceed after a change in the project's route left part of the property unused. The case concerns land in Tomball, Harris County. The state acquired it from Joyce Hutcherson, Rudolph Pusok and Jimmie Pusok in 2014. After the route changed, the state identified part of the land as surplus but refused to sell it back. The former owners later transferred their repurchase rights to JRJ Pusok Holdings LLC. The company then took the matter to court. On June 12, 2026, the state's highest court allowed the claim to proceed. However, it did not order Texas to return the land.The dispute began in October 2013. Texas notified the landowners that it intended to acquire their property for a highway project. The state initially offered $496,120 in compensation. After the offer was not accepted, condemnation proceedings began.In April 2014, both sides agreed on a value of $681,705. The property was then transferred to the state through a special warranty deed. The condemnation case was later dismissed following the settlement.Officials later changed the highway's route. As a result, part of the acquired property was left unused. In February 2017, a representative of the Texas Department of Transportation's Right of Way Division identified the land that the state considered surplus. However, the state refused to sell it back to the former owners.The landowners then transferred their repurchase rights to JRJ Pusok Holdings LLC. The company filed a lawsuit to enforce those rights under Texas law.JRJ Pusok Holdings sued the state and the director of the Texas Department of Transportation's Right of Way Division. The state argued that sovereign immunity protected it from the lawsuit. It also challenged the court's jurisdiction.A trial court initially dismissed the case. The Texas Court of Appeals for the Fourteenth District later reversed that decision on the repurchase claim. It ruled that the claim could proceed despite the state's immunity argument. Texas then appealed to the state Supreme Court.On June 12, 2026, the Texas Supreme Court upheld the appellate court's decision. It ruled that sovereign immunity could not block the statutory repurchase claim under the circumstances covered by the law.The court also clarified that property acquired through condemnation proceedings can qualify as property acquired through eminent domain. This applies even when both sides agree on compensation before a final condemnation judgment.The ruling also addressed the right to repurchase only the portion of the property that is no longer needed for public use.The case was sent back to the lower court for further proceedings. The Supreme Court did not rule that JRJ Pusok Holdings was entitled to the land. Nor did it order the state to sell the property back.Chapter 21 of the Texas Property Code provides a repurchase right in certain circumstances. This can apply when property acquired through eminent domain is no longer needed for its intended public use.However, the right is subject to specific legal conditions. These include rules on the original public use and whether the property has become unnecessary for that purpose.The Supreme Court's decision focused on whether the repurchase claim could proceed under the law. It did not establish an automatic right for all former landowners to reclaim property whenever a government project changes.
Article Summary: The Texas Supreme Court ruled that a claim to buy back land acquired for a highway can proceed after a change in the project's route left part of the property unused. The case concerns land in Tomball, Harris County. The state acquired it from Joyce Hutcherson, Rudolph Pusok and Jimmie PusOK in 2014. After the route changed, the state identified part of it as surplus but refused to sell it back. The former owners later transferred their repurchase rights to JRJ PUSok Holdings LLC. The company then took the matter to court.

Article Title: Ryan Seacrest’s foundation opened its first bilingual hospital media studio in Miami; young patients can now host broadcasts

How will Ryan Seacrest’s bilingual studio help young patients

How did young patients join Ryan Seacrest’s first Miami broadcast

How will Miami’s bilingual studio support children and families

He described the bilingual studio as a way to make the Foundation's programming accessible to more children and their families.It is the only studio that will curate content in Spanish to offer to other hospitals in the network, in line with its mission of building broadcast media centres within pediatric hospitals across the country.According to the Foundation, patients took part in the first-ever Seacrest Studios broadcast from Nicklaus Children's on opening day. Article Title: From January 1, 2027, Michigan will prohibit uncertified, untreated firewood from entering the state to keep out more than 140 pests and diseases; repeat offenders could face fines of $1,000 to $10,00
Article Text:
Michigan will allow firewood from outside the state only if it is properly treated to eliminate insects and pathogens. (AI photo)

How insects hidden in firewood can damage forests

Why ordinary dried firewood may not qualify

Fines will follow a year of public awareness

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support Michigan's new rules on firewood restrictions? Yes, it's necessary to protect our forests. No, it seems too strict. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A piece of firewood may appear harmless, but insects and plant diseases can remain hidden inside it and travel to new places when the wood is moved. A new rule in Michigan bans untreated firewood brought from outside the US state starting January 1, 2027. The restriction is intended to prevent the introduction of more than 140 plant pests and diseases. While the first year will focus on awareness, repeat offenders could face fines ranging from $1,000 to $10,000 from 2028.The Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (MDARD) announced the quarantine last month, alongside the Michigan Invasive Species Program. In the official statement, the state said the rule will apply to everyone bringing firewood across the state's borders, including campers, travellers and businesses. Firewood that has received approved heat treatment and carries the required certification will continue to be permitted.The difficulty with identifying contaminated firewood is that harmful organisms are not always visible. Insects may remain beneath the bark or deep inside the wood, while some diseases leave no obvious signs. This means that even firewood that looks normal could carry organisms capable of affecting trees elsewhere.State officials say preventing their introduction is more effective than trying to control them after an infestation has developed.Michigan has already experienced the damage invasive insects can cause. One example is the emerald ash borer, an insect associated with extensive tree mortality in the state.Emily Silver, from Michigan State University's Forestry Department, told WILX News 10 that the emerald ash borer had killed an estimated 60% to 75% of ash trees across Michigan.The problem extends beyond the immediate damage caused by insects. Trees weakened by an infestation may also become less capable of surviving other environmental pressures.“It’s sort of like human beings: anything that causes stress to the organism makes it a lot less resilient to other things that happen,” Silver told WILX.Other organisms of concern include the Asian longhorned beetle and spotted lanternfly.Michigan's new rule does not prohibit all firewood brought from outside the state. Instead, it requires imported firewood to undergo a treatment process designed to eliminate insects and pathogens.For certification, the temperature at the centre of the wood must reach at least 140 degrees Fahrenheit and remain there for 60 consecutive minutes. The treatment must also be recognised by MDARD, another state's agriculture department or the US Department of Agriculture.Simply drying firewood in a kiln will not necessarily satisfy these conditions. Although drying removes moisture, it does not establish that the wood has reached the required internal temperature for the specified duration.Some wood products are excluded from the quarantine. These include kiln-dried dimensional lumber, wood pellets and wood chips no larger than one inch in two dimensions. Certain untreated wood products sent directly to approved processing facilities are also exempt.Michigan has separately introduced a voluntary Invasive-Free Firewood Certification Program. It allows producers within the state who meet the treatment requirements to display a "Certified Invasive-Free" seal on their firewood.People bringing untreated firewood into Michigan will be subject to the new restrictions from January 2027. However, enforcement during that year will primarily involve informing the public about the requirements.MDARD will work with the Michigan Department of Natural Resources on the implementation. From January 1, 2028, violations will lead to warning letters, while repeated violations may attract fines of $1,000 to $10,000. People who voluntarily report violations may face penalties of up to $500.The authorities are also asking people to change how they purchase and use firewood. Their advice is to buy it close to where it will be burned, preferably within 10 miles, and leave any unused wood at that location rather than carrying it elsewhere.Michigan is not the first US state to impose restrictions on firewood movement. Minnesota, New York and Wisconsin have similar requirements concerning certified, heat-treated firewood entering their borders.However, the new Michigan quarantine deals specifically with wood arriving from outside the state. Silver has also raised concerns about movement within Michigan, pointing out that transporting wood between places such as Detroit and the Upper Peninsula could spread harmful organisms.
Article Summary: New rule bans untreated firewood brought from outside the US state starting January 1, 2027. The restriction is intended to prevent the introduction of more than 140 plant pests and diseases. Repeat offenders could face fines ranging from $1,000 to $10,000 from 2028.

Article Title: First ‘Survivor’ winner Richard Hatch won $1 million in 2000; now, 26 years later, court orders him to pay $3.29 million in unpaid taxes
Article Text:
Image credit: Monty Brinton/CBS

Richard Hatch is challenging the $3.29 million judgment

Previous tax evasion conviction led to prison sentence

Government alleged he transferred properties to avoid creditors

IRS rejected Hatch's settlement offers

Richard Hatch, the winner of the first season of Survivor in 2000, has been ordered to pay $3,293,471.56 to the US federal government over unpaid tax liabilities, with interest continuing to accrue. The ruling, issued on March 17, 2026, comes more than 25 years after Hatch won $1,010,000 on the reality competition show. The tax dispute involves liabilities from 2000, 2001 and 2012, and follows a lengthy history of legal battles over his finances. Hatch is challenging the latest judgment and has filed an appeal before the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. He is representing himself in the case and has said he believes a review of the full record will lead to a fair outcome.Two days after the March 17 ruling, Hatch filed a notice of appeal, signalling his intention to challenge the decision before the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. He has chosen to represent himself in the proceedings.In a statement to People, Hatch said the appeal would provide an objective review of the facts. He expressed confidence that the appellate court would examine the complete record, including evidence he believes was not adequately addressed by the lower court.Hatch also said he had spent 25 years trying to resolve the complicated situation and remained committed to reaching a fair outcome. He declined to comment further while the appeal was pending.The latest judgment follows Hatch's earlier criminal conviction over unpaid taxes. In 2006, a jury found him guilty of two counts of tax evasion involving the 2000 and 2001 tax years.He was sentenced to 51 months in prison, followed by three years of supervised release. As part of the sentence, he was required to file amended tax returns for both years and pay the outstanding amounts in full.Hatch failed to comply with those conditions and returned to prison in 2011. His earlier conviction and failure to fulfil the court's requirements form part of the lengthy legal history behind his current tax dispute.A separate part of the federal government's complaint, filed in 2022, concerned two properties Hatch allegedly transferred to his sister, Kristin Hatch, in 2003 and 2005.According to the complaint, the government alleged that the transfers were intended to hinder, delay or defraud creditors, including the US government, amid efforts to recover outstanding tax liabilities. The properties were among the assets the government said were relevant to its attempts to enforce tax liens against Hatch.The allegations formed part of the civil proceedings seeking to recover the unpaid taxes.The complaint also outlined the Internal Revenue Service's efforts to recover the outstanding amounts. In 2010, the agency sent Hatch a Notice of Deficiency concerning tax liabilities that had not previously been assessed.Hatch contested the proposed deficiencies and penalties and submitted multiple offers in compromise, which would have allowed him to settle the debt for less than the full amount owed. The government rejected those proposals.In 2012, a stipulated decision was entered in the tax dispute. According to the government's complaint, the decision barred Hatch from contesting those liabilities further. The latest judgment subsequently established the amount he owes, while his appeal seeks to challenge the court's decision.
Article Summary: Richard Hatch has been ordered to pay $3,293,471.56 to the US federal government. The ruling, issued on March 17, 2026, comes more than 25 years after Hatch won $1,010,000 on the reality competition show. The tax dispute involves liabilities from 2000, 2001 and 2012, and follows a lengthy history of legal battles over his finances. Hatch is challenging the latest judgment and has filed an appeal before the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit.

Article Title: In 2007, a couple gave $1.5 million to revive UNLV's dead debate programme; 11 years later, it was ranked No. 5 in America
Article Text:
The Las Vegas Strip can be seen in the distance from various points on the UNLV campus. Image Credit: Wikipedia

How did a $1.5 million gift revive UNLV's debate programme

The team established itself among the nation's leading competitors

The 2016-2017 student members and coaching staff of the UNLV Debate Team, which ended the fall semester ranked eleventh in the US. Image Credit: UNLV/Website

Intensive preparation helped turn potential into results

A culture of teamwork strengthened the programme

In 2007, a $1.5 million donation from Sanford and Sandra Berman helped bring the University of Nevada, Las Vegas (UNLV) debate programme back to life after nearly a decade without a team. What followed was a remarkable rise in competitive university debating, driven by dedicated students, coaching and a growing record of tournament victories. By March 2018, just 11 years after the programme's revival, UNLV had climbed to 5th place in the national varsity rankings, establishing itself among the leading college debate teams in the US.The university's debate team had a successful history before financial difficulties brought its activities to an end. Budget cuts led to the programme being dismantled in 1998, leaving UNLV without a competitive team for almost a decade.According to the university, the turning point came in 2007 when Dr Sanford and Sandra Berman contributed $1.5 million to revive the programme. Their support helped the university rebuild its team and recruit Jacob Thompson, a communication studies professor who became its coach and director.The donation gave the programme the opportunity to develop again, but establishing a nationally competitive team required more than financial backing.Students needed to develop their research, speaking and debating abilities while building the discipline required to compete against experienced university teams.Thompson's ambition was to create a team capable of winning a national championship while maintaining a strong commitment to teamwork and representing the university responsibly. That approach became an important part of the programme's development.UNLV's progress became evident within its first few years of returning to competition. In January 2012, the university announced that its Sanford I. Berman Debate Team had entered the top 10 varsity programmes nationally for the first time.According to the university, the team was tied for 10th place with Kansas State University in the National Debate Tournament rankings. It also held the highest ranking in District I, which included universities in California, Arizona and Nevada.The achievement was particularly significant because the programme had existed in its revived form for only 5 years. It demonstrated that UNLV could compete with established institutions and gave the team a stronger position in the national debating community.The university provided another example of that progress. UNLV students Sara Beth Brooks and Matt Gomez won the Las Vegas Classic Invitational Collegiate Debate Tournament, defeating a team from the University of Texas in the final.The competition featured 98 teams from 31 colleges and universities across the western and midwestern United States. Three other UNLV teams also advanced beyond the preliminary rounds into the elimination stage.Competitive policy debating requires participants to understand complicated subjects, construct convincing arguments and respond quickly to opposing views. At UNLV, two-person teams are expected to argue both for and against a proposed policy, giving them experience in examining an issue from different perspectives.Competitors can deliver arguments at approximately 350 to 400 words per minute, considerably faster than an ordinary conversation. The speed allows them to present numerous arguments within the time available, but it also demands extensive preparation.By March 2018, the team's training and competitive experience had produced impressive results. Senior Matthew Gomez and junior Jeffrey Horn won 71 of their 92 debates during the regular season and secured 2 tournament titles.Their performance placed the pair 3rd in the national individual team rankings. UNLV itself stood 5th in the varsity standings, ahead of established competitors including Cornell, Northwestern and Baylor.Gomez and Horn earned automatic qualification for the 2018 National Debate Tournament. Another UNLV pair, senior Roman Kezios and junior Reece Aguilar, qualified after winning the Pacific Champions Debate Tournament in February.The university's rise was not built around a single successful partnership. By 2018, the squad consisted of eight 2-person teams, with competitors participating at novice, junior varsity and varsity levels according to their experience.The team's preparation involved substantial time outside regular classes. Gomez and Horn spent approximately 40 to 50 hours each week refining arguments, reviewing evidence and preparing for competition, with their workload increasing before major tournaments.Thompson attributed the programme's improvement to a positive atmosphere, shared effort and the team's growing history of success. The approach also created opportunities for students who had never debated before. Thompson emphasised that undergraduates from different academic backgrounds could join the programme if they were prepared to work hard and develop their abilities.The university explains that alumni have gone on to work in higher education, law, politics and both the public and private sectors. The programme also aims to encourage informed public discussion and improve access to debating opportunities for younger students. Through its summer debate camp, the team mentors middle and high school pupils, helping hundreds of young debaters develop their skills.
Article Summary: The University of Nevada, Las Vegas debate programme was dismantled in 1998. A $1.5 million donation from Sanford and Sandra Berman helped bring the programme back to life in 2007. By March 2018, UNLV had climbed to 5th place in the national varsity rankings.

Article Title: 'Who wants to take the chance?': Why Trump wants Netanyahu to stay in power in Israel
Article Text:
Trump described Netanyahu as a “Great Warrior Prime Minister”

"Great Warrior Prime Minister”

Trump said Netanyahu was a leader Israel could rely on

US President Donald Trump on Sunday explained why he endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s reelection bid, saying their strong relationship and shared approach to the war against Iran were key factors.In a phone interview with Axios, Trump said he had planned to back Netanyahu earlier but waited for the right moment, issuing his endorsement just nine days before Israel’s October 27 elections.“I was always going to do that. I just didn't want to do it too soon,” he added.Trump said Netanyahu was a leader Israel could rely on and suggested that a change in leadership could affect Washington’s role in the conflict with Iran.In a Truth Social post, he described Netanyahu as a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” and warned that if Israel had the wrong leader, the US might have to handle the work in Iran itself.The endorsement comes at a crucial time for Netanyahu, whose coalition is projected by most polls to fall short of the 61 seats required to form a government. Trump’s public backing could strengthen the Israeli prime minister’s position ahead of the election.The move also marks a shift in Trump’s recent approach to Netanyahu. The US president had previously held back from endorsing him amid tensions over the wars in Iran and Gaza.According to Axios, Trump had privately criticised Netanyahu over Israel’s failure to prevent the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks and questioned whether the prime minister was hurting Israel’s international standing.Netanyahu welcomed Trump’s backing, writing on X, “Together we will complete the mission.” His main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, meanwhile, said Israel’s elections were a domestic matter and that the country’s citizens would decide their outcome.
Article Summary: Trump said Netanyahu was a leader Israel could rely on and suggested that a change in leadership could affect Washington’s role in the conflict with Iran. The endorsement comes at a crucial time for Netanyahu, whose coalition is projected by most polls to fall short of the 61 seats required to form a government.

Article Title: Texas landowners challenge $46 billion border wall as separate lawsuit halts construction in Big Bend
Article Text:
Representative Image of a Texas rancher standing before a border wall, conflicted by its impact on land and the environment (AI-generated image)

Big Bend border wall project: $7.5 billion plan and why Texas is different

Texas landowners’ border wall lawsuit: eminent domain and the construction pause

Big Bend landowners and local officials oppose construction

A $46 billion plan to expand the US-Mexico border wall is facing resistance from Texas landowners, while a separate lawsuit has halted construction in the Big Bend region. On October 2, 2026, US District Judge Kathleen Cardone of the Western District of Texas, in El Paso, granted a preliminary injunction in a case brought by the Center for Biological Diversity, Friends of the Ruidosa Church and river guide Danny Miller Jr. The order blocks specified construction activities while the case proceeds and stays the federal waivers used to expedite the project. Separately, the No Big Bend Wall Coalition, which says its network includes more than 200 landowners, has challenged the administration’s plans. The disputes concern federal authority, private property, environmental protections and the need for border barriers in a region with comparatively few Border Patrol arrests.The $46 billion figure comes from funding approved by Republicans in 2025 as part of a broader immigration enforcement package, according to Associated Press reporting published by ABC News. The administration’s plan covers the roughly 2,000-mile US-Mexico border and includes walls, vehicle barriers, patrol roads and surveillance technology. The first border wall panels in the Big Bend region went up in mid-September 2026, although ground-disturbing work in Big Bend National Park had been documented as early as August.The administration plans to spend $7.5 billion to strengthen border infrastructure along a stretch of more than 500 miles. The region accounts for roughly one-quarter of the entire US-Mexico border, but its geography differs from that of more heavily developed border areas.Parts of the Rio Grande run below steep limestone cliffs, while remote stretches are accessible only by rocky trails and through difficult desert terrain. Supporters of the project argue that walls, vehicle barriers, patrol roads and surveillance technology are needed to deter crossings and smuggling. The administration has also warned that leaving gaps in border infrastructure could push illegal crossings and smuggling toward less fortified areas. Border Patrol arrest figures cited by AP illustrate the difference in enforcement activity across the region. In August 2026, agents arrested 8,870 people along the entire southern border, including 161 in the Big Bend sector. These figures measure arrests, not the total number of attempted crossings. Opponents argue that the region’s natural barriers and comparatively low number of arrests make an extensive wall unnecessary. Some local law enforcement officials have advocated surveillance towers and drones as alternatives. Customs and Border Protection has said it is building an average of about 12 miles of barrier per week and recently passed 200 miles of new barriers built during President Donald Trump’s second term, according to AP. The administration says the infrastructure is part of its wider effort to maintain low levels of illegal border crossings.Texas presents a particular challenge for federal construction because much of the land along the border is privately or state-owned. The government must obtain authorisation to enter private property for surveys and construction. When owners refuse access, federal authorities can pursue eminent domain, the process through which the government takes private property for public use in exchange for compensation. According to AP reporting on the legal disputes, courts have generally deferred to the government in eminent domain cases, and earlier lawsuits seeking to stop border wall projects have largely failed. A Justice Department official who spoke to AP on condition of anonymity said the Customs and Border Protection had reached agreements with dozens of Big Bend landowners. Across the southern border, about 70 cases had been referred to the department during Trump’s second term, with 50 resolved and none requiring a trial, the official said.The No Big Bend Wall Coalition has separately challenged the project, arguing that the Department of Homeland Security is misusing its authority in a region with limited illegal cross-border activity. The coalition’s lawsuit is distinct from the case that produced the October 2 injunction. That injunction was granted by US District Judge Kathleen Cardone in a lawsuit brought by the Center for Biological Diversity, Friends of the Ruidosa Church and Big Bend river guide and landowner Danny Miller Jr. The plaintiffs challenged the federal government’s use of waivers to bypass environmental and other laws to accelerate construction. The preliminary injunction covers the Big Bend Border Patrol Sector within one mile of the Rio Grande, as well as Big Bend National Park and Big Bend Ranch State Park. It also stays the relevant federal waivers while the case proceeds. The order remains in effect until the court resolves the case on its merits, unless it is modified or stayed. As of October 15, 2026, the Trump administration was seeking to suspend the injunction while pursuing Supreme Court review. In a court filing reported by Marfa Public Radio on October 9, the government asked Judge Cardone to suspend the order and said it intended to seek relief from the Supreme Court. Inside Climate News reported on October 15 that Justice Department attorneys were continuing to pursue that course.Resistance extends beyond the courtroom. Landowners and business owners have attended county meetings, protested against proposed agreements with contractors and monitored construction areas for possible violations. Some have urged local authorities not to provide land or road access to companies working on the project. In Terrell County, residents unsuccessfully opposed leasing airport land to a barrier contractor. In Jeff Davis County, a proposed agreement allowing another contractor to use a county road had not been approved at the time of AP’s reporting. Terrell County Judge Dale Lynn Carruthers said the county had limited control over the federal project and suggested that refusing the lease might simply lead the contractor to find another location.Opposition has also come from some Republicans. Rancher Laura Allen, who said she voted for Trump twice, supports securing the border but believes spending billions on barriers in Big Bend is unnecessary. Terrell County Sheriff Thad Cleveland, a former Border Patrol agent, has argued that drones and surveillance towers are more suitable for the rugged terrain he patrols. Republican Sen. John Cornyn has pressed the Department of Homeland Security about Texans’ concerns following bulldozing in Big Bend National Park. Local opponents have raised concerns about the effects of construction on tourism, access to the Rio Grande and ranching operations. Some residents and property owners have also expressed concern about the consequences for the region’s natural environment.The Zuberbueler family, whose Val Verde County ranch dates to 1898, is concerned about the effect of construction on livestock and water supplies. The family raises Angora goats and Rambouillet sheep on land extending toward the Rio Grande. Although the animals can pass through vehicle barriers, the family says the barriers could prevent cowboys from moving freely across the property. Earlier border wall disputes provide historical context for the use of eminent domain. A 2017 ProPublica investigation reported that the Department of Homeland Security filed more than 360 eminent domain lawsuits in less than a year after 2007 across Texas, New Mexico, Arizona and California. Some landowners remained involved in court proceedings for years. The immediate future of the Big Bend project depends in part on the ongoing legal proceedings. The temporary order has halted construction while the administration challenges it, but it does not by itself resolve the broader dispute over federal authority, property access or the merits of building a wall across the region. The court proceedings will determine how the legal challenge proceeds as landowners and officials continue to contest the project.
Article Summary: The administration plans to spend $7.5 billion to strengthen border infrastructure along a stretch of more than 500 miles. The first border wall panels in the Big Bend region went up in mid-September 2026, although ground- disturbing work in Big Bend National Park had been documented as early as August. The No Big Bend Wall Coalition has separately challenged the project, arguing that the Department of Homeland Security is misusing its authority in a region with limited illegal cross-border activity.

Article Title: A San Francisco couple built a Buddhist meditation sanctuary in their backyard, but a planning complaint put it at risk
Article Text:
PC: San Francisco Chronicle

Why did a San Francisco couple’s meditation sanctuary face a complaint

PC: San Francisco Chronicle

Why did San Francisco’s meditation sanctuary violate planning rules

How could new zoning rules protect San Francisco’s backyard sanctuary

What happens next in the backyard sanctuary zoning dispute

Why are San Francisco residents struggling with building permits

A San Francisco couple is fighting to save their Buddhist meditation sanctuary after an anonymous planning complaint raised concerns about violations of city building rules. Sam Geffner and Mar Rodin built the backyard retreat in their Noe Valley home, completing construction around 2008. The structure, inspired by traditional Japanese architecture, features a meditation room, skylights and deep roof eaves. After using the space for more than a decade, the couple faced the prospect of demolishing it or altering its design. Having spent nearly $30,000 on architects and lawyers, they are now hoping a proposed change to city planning rules will save their sanctuary.According to the San Francisco Chronicle, the sanctuary stands behind the couple’s rainbow-painted house on Clipper Street in San Francisco. Gently curving stone steps lead to a meditation room built into the sloping hillside, with two skylights allowing natural light into the space. Sliding glass doors open towards a rocky grotto where koi fish swim.The building’s design draws on traditional Japanese architecture, featuring timber framing, a high roof and wide eaves. Geffner has meditated there for nearly 20 years and described its purpose to the San Francisco Chronicle, saying, “It’s a space that separates you from the everyday world.”The couple regard the structure as a refuge connected to their Buddhist meditation practice.Geffner and Rodin began considering a redesign of their backyard around 25 years ago. They hired landscape designer Kent Gordon England, who designed the meditation room and koi pond. According to Geffner, England assured them that they did not need to worry about obtaining permits for such a small addition.Construction was completed around 2008, and the couple used the space for more than a decade without encountering problems. That changed in 2019, when an anonymous complaint was made to San Francisco’s Planning Department alleging that the structure violated city rules. Geffner described the experience as “a rude awakening”, while Rodin said, “We were really trusting in our cowboy.” England did not respond to the newspaper’s request for comment.San Francisco’s planning code regulates the size and design of backyard buildings. The rules are intended to preserve open spaces within city blocks and protect natural light and ventilation for neighbouring properties. The couple’s architect acknowledged at the hearing that the room exceeds the height and floor-area requirements.One of the central issues is the building’s roof overhang. The planning code permits a maximum roof overhang of 12 inches, whereas the sanctuary has eaves extending four feet beyond its walls. Those deep eaves are an important feature of the building’s traditional architectural design and part of the couple’s argument for retaining it.After years of uncertainty, Geffner and Rodin appealed to the city’s zoning administrator for an exemption in the summer of 2026. At a hearing, an architect representing the couple argued that an exception should be considered because the structure is built into a hillside and is used as part of their Buddhist faith.Explaining the significance of the design, Geffner told the hearing, “In Buddhist tradition, the peaked roofs and deep eaves are understood as this building’s primary way of signalling this is a sacred, protected space.” The couple also sought support from their neighbours, going door to door and distributing a 13-page packet of photographs documenting the backyard and meditation room. Geffner said they received more than 30 letters of support.The dispute has attracted the attention of Rafael Mandelman, the supervisor representing the district that includes Noe Valley. At a meeting of San Francisco’s Board of Supervisors in September 2026, he introduced a proposed change to the planning code that would allow backyard structures built before 2010 to remain, provided they fell within the scope of the proposed measure.The proposal would extend an existing provision that grandfathered in backyard buildings constructed before 2003. If approved, the revised cut-off date would cover the couple’s sanctuary, which was completed around 2008. Mandelman said the length of time a structure had existed without causing a problem should be considered when deciding whether it needed to be removed.“You look at it and think, ‘That can’t be right,’” Mandelman said of the couple’s predicament, according to the San Francisco Chronicle. He added that it should not be necessary for homeowners to spend years and substantial sums of money trying to secure permission to keep such a structure. The newspaper reported that the number of backyard buildings that could qualify under the proposed change was not yet clear.Patrick Hannan, a spokesperson for San Francisco’s recently merged planning and building inspection departments, said planning staff had worked with Mandelman on the proposal. In a statement quoted by the newspaper, Hannan said, “Our job is to balance priorities when they conflict in the real world.” He described the proposed amendment as “a targeted way to let the small meditation space stay while ensuring that the interior-block open space will be preserved. ”The zoning administrator, Corey Teague, told the couple at the hearing that he would consider their arguments and respond later. According to Hannan, Teague has remained in regular contact with the couple’s architect, although Geffner and Rodin had not received a final decision at the time of the San Francisco Chronicle report.Mandelman’s proposed ordinance is expected to go before the full Board of Supervisors in the coming months. If it passes, it would supersede the zoning administrator’s determination on the matter. If it does not pass, the couple could still receive an exemption from the zoning administrator. They would also have the option to appeal an unfavourable decision, although that process would probably increase their costs.The case comes amid wider difficulties faced by San Francisco residents navigating the city’s planning and building regulations. The San Francisco Chronicle reported that even Supervisor Myrna Melgar, a former president of the San Francisco Planning Commission, had previously described struggling to establish whether she needed a permit to replace a backyard gazebo.For now, Geffner and Rodin intend to continue using the meditation room while they await the outcome of the planning process. The sanctuary has remained part of their lives for decades, and its future depends on the outcome of the proposed code change or the decision on their exemption request. Reflecting on the role meditation plays in dealing with uncertainty, Geffner told the San Francisco Chronicle, “Meditation is a way of bringing a little control over what’s out of control. Reminding you not to take it too seriously.”
Article Summary: Sam Geffner and Mar Rodin built the backyard retreat in their Noe Valley home, completing construction around 2008. The structure features a meditation room, skylights and deep roof eaves. After using the space for more than a decade, the couple faced the prospect of demolishing it or altering its design. They are now hoping a proposed change to city planning rules will save their sanctuary.

Article Title: An 18-year-old built an AI traffic system that changes pedestrian signals based on how safe people feel crossing a road
Article Text:
Phillips Academy student Jay Jung of Massachusetts. Image Credit: Impacto Positivo

How does the 18-year-old's AI traffic system make pedestrian crossings safer

Image Credit: Jay Jing/NiceNews

The idea began with a problem involving his grandparents

SmartBlink adjusts crossing time for speed of walking

The student received international recognition for his invention

An 18-year-old student has developed an AI-powered traffic system designed to make road crossings safer for people who need more time to reach the other side. The system is called SmartBlink and instead of a set time for crossing, it changes the pedestrian light timings based on how fast people cross the road. The invention, developed by Phillips Academy student Jay Jung of Massachusetts, aims to make streets more accessible to older adults and others with physical difficulties.
